endorsements.quote: Before LLM-based systems are trusted for medical education—even those including algorithmic components to mitigate bias—they will require validation by human experts who have training in recognizing structural and systemic biases to avoid unintentionally propagating biases to medical learners via AI.

unlisted_practices: Insist that LLM-based medical education tools undergo validation to quantify the degree to which hallucination affects performance.
Keep humans in the loop at all times when using AI for evaluation of learners, and do not surrender evaluative authority to an algorithm.
Select LLMs that can be used in an economically sustainable way, balancing cost, security, and performance when choosing between local and cloud-based LLMs.

Ensure adequate data security provisions under HIPAA and FERPA before transmitting data to cloud-based LLM providers, and consider on-premises local LLMs to minimize transmission of protected information.
Consult local institutional experts when making security-related decisions about LLM use.
Validate AI-augmented narrative feedback systems to ensure they are acceptable to faculty and students and do not increase bias or decrease feedback quality.
Validate LLM-based simulations with respect to hallucination and bias and subject them to economic cost-benefit analysis.
Focus initial LLM-assisted qualitative coding on tasks using coding schemas strongly backed by existing theory, because of the hallucination problem.
Medical educators should stay aware of the changing legal and regulatory landscape regarding copyright and LLM use.
Prioritize research on whether LLMs improve learning outcomes beyond satisfaction, including knowledge transfer, learner behavior, and patient outcomes.
Foster cross-disciplinary collaboration among clinicians, educators, computer scientists, engineers, ethicists, and diversity, equity, and inclusion experts to build AI-enabled medical education.

screen.reason: This is a commentary/perspective article discussing limitations (hallucination, bias, cost, security), potential applications, and approaches/recommendations for using generative AI in primary care medical education.
